mainEntity.name: How long should I sleep with my head elevated after dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental professionals recommend keeping the head elevated for at least the first three to five nights following surgery. This is the period during which post-operative swelling tends to be most significant. You can gradually return to your normal sleeping position once swelling has noticeably reduced. However, it is advisable to continue avoiding sleeping directly on the treated side for a few weeks as the soft tissue continues to heal. Your dental team will provide guidance tailored to your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Can sleeping on my side damage a dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: A successfully placed dental implant is secured within the jawbone and is unlikely to be dislodged solely by sleeping on your side. However, sleeping on the same side as the implant site in the early post-operative days may increase localised swelling, pressure, and discomfort. It is a sensible precaution to avoid this position during the initial healing phase. Once healing is well established, normal sleep positions are generally comfortable and appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel discomfort at night after implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of discomfort at night is common, particularly in the first few days following surgery. The surgical site remains sensitive during this period, and lying down can sometimes intensify the sensation of pressure or throbbing. Following the pain management advice provided by your dental team, maintaining head elevation, and applying a cold compress during waking hours can help. If pain is severe, persistent, or worsening after the third day, it is worth contacting your dental practice for assessment.

mainEntity.name: What foods can I eat while recovering from dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: During the initial recovery period — typically the first week — soft foods that require minimal chewing are recommended. Examples include yoghurt, mashed potato, scrambled eggs, soup (not too hot), smoothies, and soft cooked vegetables. Hard, crunchy, chewy, or very hot foods should be avoided, as they may disturb the surgical site or the healing clot. As healing progresses and your dental team confirms it is appropriate, you can gradually reintroduce a more varied diet.

mainEntity.name: Does grinding my teeth at night affect implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Teeth grinding (bruxism) can place considerable force on the jaw and dental structures during sleep. In the context of implant healing, repeated excessive pressure on or near the implant site may potentially interfere with osseointegration. If you are known to grind your teeth, it is important to inform your dental team before and after surgery. A custom-made night guard may be recommended to help protect the implant and surrounding teeth during the healing period and beyond.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my dental implant is healing correctly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Signs that healing is progressing well include a gradual reduction in swelling and discomfort over the first week, the absence of fever or signs of infection, and a stable, secure feel at the implant site. Your dental team will schedule follow-up appointments to monitor healing directly, often including a post-operative dental examination. If you notice increasing pain, swelling that is not improving, an unpleasant taste, or any movement at the implant site, it is advisable to contact your practice promptly so that appropriate assessment can be carried out.
